fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Sacred Numbers and the One Ring", "body": "Chance opens on the numbers packed into the first chapter of The Fellowship of the Ring, Bilbo's eleventy-first birthday and Frodo's coming of age at 33, and Becca argues nothing in Tolkien is accidental. Drawing on the Pythagorean lineage of Western archetypal astrology, she treats number as qualitative, tracing the three, seven, nine and one of the ring poem into the seven stars, seven stones, white tree and nine ships of Númenor. She reads the One Ring as a perverse inversion of sacred unity that tries to homogenize difference, while Chance contrasts it with the hero who individuates into a true one."}, {"title": "Atlantis and Tolkien's Great Wave Dream", "body": "Becca recounts the recurring dream Tolkien described from around age seven, a great wave drowning the land, which he later called his Atlantis haunting. She follows it through The Lost Road, the time travel story he began after a pact with C.S. Lewis, and The Notion Club Papers, where she says a storm foretold for 1987 was later matched by Christopher Tolkien to England's great storm that year. The dream finally settled into the drowning of Númenor behind Aragorn's lineage and Faramir's dream, and Chance takes the episode as a sign, in his view, that imagination can glimpse past and future."}, {"title": "Jung, Tolkien and Their Two Red Books", "body": "Becca's dissertation traces parallels between Carl Jung's Red Book, begun in 1913, and the legendarium Tolkien started in the same years, framed in his fiction as the Red Book of Westmarch, even though the two men never met. She points out that Jung wrote his Seven Sermons to the Dead in 1916, three years before Tolkien's first cosmogony. For her, synchronicities between the two that she says outside influence cannot explain opened the idea that imagination gives access to a real imaginal realm, neither physical nor made up but participatory, an idea she hears in Sufism, Neoplatonism and Gnosticism."}, {"title": "Melkor's Discord and the Roots of Evil", "body": "Becca retells the Ainulindalë, where Ilúvatar gives the Ainur a theme to adorn in song, Melkor weaves in his own discordant theme, and a third, sorrowful theme folds that discord into the whole before the music becomes a vision of the world. In the myth, water still carries that first music, which is why, she suggests, the sea calls to us. She reads Melkor's secret shame and anger as the seed of Morgoth and Sauron, while Chance frames the secret fire as awareness itself and argues evil only twists what already exists, a scavenger rather than a source."}, {"title": "Imagination as Discovery, Not Invention", "body": "Working from Coleridge's Biographia Literaria, Becca separates the primary imagination, the divine creativity behind all perception, from the secondary imagination of the human artist and from mere fancy. Tolkien's essay On Fairy-Stories reframes this as sub-creation: images arise, art shapes them, and fantasy adds strangeness and wonder. She describes Tolkien less as a god of Middle-earth than a witness and translator, a devout Catholic who felt creative work carried creation forward. Chance adds that Ilúvatar simply sings what he sees, and Becca closes on art as surrender, gestated like a child rather than controlled, with enchantment lying beyond the creator."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Becca Tarnas is the author of Journey To The Imaginal Realm: A Reader's Guide To J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings. As a PhD scholar of philosophy and religion, Becca guides us through the deep symbolic archive and wisdom of Tolkien's great works. In this episode we explore the source of human imagination, the Atlantis mystery in Middle-Earth, the parallels between Carl Jung and Tolkien, and the mechanism by which great stories are able to immerse us in an enchanted other-world.

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Invention as discovery and art as surrender", "body": "Becca Tarnas carries her thoughts on creative surrender into the members' section, sharing a point she learned from Tolkien scholar Tom Shippey: the word invent traces back to a Latin root meaning to discover, so every invention may be a finding of something already present in an archetypal realm. Chance Garton calls the idea liberating and adds his own observation about the blank canvas. In his view, people who think they are not creative freeze before the whole, while artists simply begin, making one choice at a time and weaving outward, bringing the infinite through piece by piece."}, {"title": "Stars, wonder and the evening star Eärendil", "body": "Chance Garton notes that the first elves woke under starlight, before sun or moon, and asks what that liminal beginning means. Becca Tarnas links stars, language and water as pointers back to creation, quoting cosmologist Brian Swimme that the stars lead us to wonder, both in awe and in the urge to understand. She then traces Eärendil from a line in an Anglo-Saxon poem that gave Tolkien a curious thrill in 1913, through Númenor to Aragorn and Arwen. As Venus, she says, this star of love keeps giving hope to characters at their darkest moments."}, {"title": "Syzygy, polarity and a plural hero's journey", "body": "Chance Garton asks how Jung might read the syzygy, the union of solar and lunar, in Tolkien's paired lovers. Becca Tarnas offers what she calls a possibly controversial view: that polarities still matter, but naming lunar qualities feminine and solar qualities masculine may hold people back from developing both. She then argues that Tolkien gives us a hero's plural journey in which nobody acts alone, from Frodo and Sam to the community scouring the Shire. Chance Garton agrees that gender and polarity are not the same thing, warning that confusing them leads to demonizing one side or the other."}, {"title": "Saruman, industry and our relationship to the earth", "body": "Quoting Gandalf's line that he who breaks a thing to find out what it is has left the path of wisdom, Chance Garton asks about Saruman and reductionism. Becca Tarnas connects it to Tolkien's move from rural Sarehole to industrial Birmingham and the loss of his mother, saying he always took the side of the trees. She reads Saruman's oddly modern speech as a portrait of an exploiting mindset and compares ecological crises to the Ents rising against him. When Chance Garton raises self-reliance away from cities, Becca points to privilege and to community efforts like urban gardens in Detroit."}, {"title": "Bombadil, the Barrow and memories that are not ours", "body": "Becca Tarnas calls Tom Bombadil the one true anomaly in a world where Tolkien explains every origin, noting that Goldberry only says he is. Her own playful theory is that Bombadil may be a figure of Tolkien himself, an old, fatherless witness singing within his own small world. Chance Garton suggests he might be read as a fully individuated Self. They turn to the Barrow-downs, where Merry seems to inhabit a dead man's memory, which Becca discusses through Verlyn Flieger's essay. Chance Garton wonders whether something like psychometry through the enchanted blade could explain it, while both leave the question open."}]

fields.Plus Quotes JSON: [{"text": "So to invent actually comes from the root of discovery and that all inventions really are simply discoveries of something that maybe already exists in some archetypal realm.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "And so how fitting that it's the symbol of love, Venus, or in this mythology, Eärendil, that again and again provides hope to each one of the characters, as they encounter their greatest trials.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What has been seen as a binary or a dichotomy can be recognized as a spectrum. And when we look at polarity, we have to recognize that there's something in between holding them together.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "What Tolkien is giving us is a hero's plural journey. And if you look at the Lord of the Rings, no character does anything alone. Frodo can't go to Mordor without Sam, or without Gollum, for that matter.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "So I think that it is important that we parse out the difference between gender and polarity, because they're not the same thing. They really aren't.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Saruman is a representation of that 20th century industrializing mindset that sees the earth as something that can simply be exploited and put to use.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "I think more importantly than getting out and going somewhere to find wholeness is to return to where we started with new eyes and be able to see the infinite potential that's there in that space.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/a784fd99-3e6f-436c-a8f3-c4f913b855ed/profile-pic.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Tom Bombadil, the only explanation that we get about him is from Goldberry, his wife, and she says he is. And that's not much of an explanation.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
fields.Quotes JSON: [{"text": "The imagination is actually something that gives us access to a real place, the imaginal realm, that is not physical, it is not simply abstract, it is most definitely not made up.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "Like all universal principles in our cosmos, the truth seems to be founded on paradox.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "A fantasy for Tolkien isn't something that's made up. It's something that has organically emerged through one and actually been discovered, and then shaped and honed by the artist.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The reason we feel that longing at the edge of the sea, and that calling for the sea, is because we're remembering creation when we hear it.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "The only thing that makes the shadow or the darkness frightening or threatening is that we don't know what it is.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "Nothing in Tolkien's accidental. He has revised and edited and so carefully shaped the material coming through him.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}, {"text": "It's not up to us to slay the dragon or defeat the Dark Lord. It's up to us to maintain the small acts of goodness and kindness and decency that we're capable of doing.", "author": "Chance Garton", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/aa717e55-9487-4255-a7df-3f8ef10940c4/Chance+Garton+Patreon+Portrait.png?content-type=image%2Fpng"}, {"text": "The enchantment lies in what is inherently beyond us. We as creators are actually along for the journey as much as everyone else in the story.", "author": "Becca Tarnas", "portrait": "https://images.squarespace-cdn.com/content/5987d897cf81e0278ec5322e/9c49afcc-b006-43d8-bd19-321ad901f98b/BECCA-TARNAS.jpg?content-type=image%2Fjpeg"}]
